explanation: No clear shared feature. It fires strongly on tokens in the middle of code identifiers or strings ("User Id", ThreadPool, attendees, menuItemStyle, remote_user), on long whitespace runs in legal case captions, on footnote markers [^1], and on scattered function words in prose. Moderate and weak hits are mostly random prose and medical word pieces.

Fires on the start of an uncommon proper name or surname, especially a capital 'K' token after a first name or initial (Klobuchar, Knaus, Kuhn, KRAUSE), and on the first word piece of non-English words in Danish, Hungarian or Swedish text. A weaker offshoot fires on verbs like 'are' or 'has' after a plural subject in English prose.

Fires on word pieces in the middle of words or on function words in non-English text: Russian, Turkish, Japanese, Swedish, Portuguese, Spanish, French, Dutch and Romanian. It is strongest in Russian, Turkish and Japanese, and moderate in other European languages. English text gives almost no activation.

Fires on the second or later piece of a multi-token proper name for an institution or place, especially foreign or Asian ones (Seoul National, China National Knowledge, Bharatiya Janata, Tianjin, Ben-Gurion, Zend Technologies), and on similar pieces of fixed technical names (linux/kernel, Content-Transfer). Ordinary common words do not activate it.

Fires on boilerplate tokens in formal or templated documents: license headers (distributing, name, decompiled), court opinion headers (Decided, Argued, Circuit Judge, PENNSYLVANIA), email headers (Sent:), and path or code template pieces (Users, USER, '=', ')'). It also fires on a few unrelated prose tokens.

Fires on the word right after a superlative, ordinal or 'ever/never' expression, which completes a 'first X', 'Nth all-time', 'never tried' or 'ever eaten' record or first-time claim (first title, first woman, first ... to, ever recorded, oldest). A weaker offshoot fires on 'case' in 'we report the case of'.

Fires on the token 'head' and its variants (<head> in HTML, Head-teacher, headache, heady, HEAD) and, about as strongly, on the 'ros' or 'r' piece of 'electrospray' or 'electrification'. It also fires on a few unrelated word pieces (Addis Ababa, farcical, preliminary).

Fires on tokens in formal academic or institutional prose. It is strongest on the 'of' in 'Department of' in author affiliations, on institution nouns (University, hospital, National Guard), and on hedged or evaluative scientific words (relatively, dominant, ensure, investigated). Casual text barely activates it.

Fires on the final piece of a number or of an unusual proper name: the last digit of a price, year or model number (1,209.99, 1967, 40,000, BMP180), or the closing piece of a foreign place or person name (Torvalds, Babruysk, Khaleda, Kyaw). It also fires on closing punctuation after such names.

No single theme. It fires on content words in the middle of a phrase in varied prose (RNA polymerase, protects, hidden, rights, exoplanet, 'no choice but', 'get away', 'under the cover'), with no consistent lexical or syntactic trigger.

A mixture. It fires on '::' and ':=' in code, on pieces of numbers, DOIs and coordinates, on punctuation like '(' or '/' after a dateline or number, and on assorted prose words (operating, camel, moderate, biofilms).

A mixture. It fires on the comma inside unified-diff hunk headers (@@ -281,7 +281,11), on number pieces in arithmetic and chemical formulas, on the second word of fixed noun phrases (greatest common divisor, single women, its association), and on various prose words.

Fires on a generic category noun that follows an adjective or modifier and names a kind of thing: organ (in organ function or fibrosis), language, browser, Court (in 'Court of Appeal'), Month, IDE, edition, antibiotic. It is strongest when the noun is the head of a technical or institutional term.

A mixture. It fires on template or shell syntax tokens ('{%' and '%' in Django templates, the '-' before a find or cgo flag, quotes and brackets in code), on pieces in the middle of multi-word organization names (United Nations Educational, Provincial, National Security), on Japanese political or katakana tokens, and on scattered function words.
